sections.title: The Blessings over Fragrance
sections.html:
Just as there is a mitzva to recite a blessing over every food a person eats, so too there is a mitzva to recite a blessing over the enjoyment of a pleasant fragrance. And although the enjoyment of fragrance is more spiritual, the Sages instituted a blessing over it, for a person is forbidden to derive benefit from this world without a blessing (Berakhot 35a; above 1:2). They also learned this from the verse (Tehillim 150:6): "Let every soul (neshama) praise the Lord, Halleluya" – "What is it from which the soul derives enjoyment and the body does not derive enjoyment? You must say, this is fragrance" (Berakhot 43b). Thus one must praise God for the enjoyment of fragrance. But the Sages did not institute a blessing over the enjoyment of hearing a pleasant sound or seeing a beautiful sight, because from these enjoyments no substance enters a person's body, whereas in the enjoyment of fragrance, particles of the fragrance enter the body (MB 216:4).

However, they did not institute a final blessing over fragrance, since after one stops smelling, the pleasure departs and nothing of it remains (SA OḤ 216:1).

Through this blessing we learn to pay attention to the subtle and delicate things that God created in the world, which also give a person pleasure and enrich his feelings. And since the Sages said that the soul enjoys fragrance, a pleasant fragrance can awaken the faith within the soul, strengthen a person's spiritual powers, and awaken in him desire and longing to rise to a high level, above and beyond tangible things.

In order that the thanksgiving be complete and precise, the Sages instituted a special blessing for each type of fragrance, according to the substance from which the fragrance emanates. There are five blessings:

a) Over a fragrance emanating from a species of tree, one recites: "Barukh Ata Hashem Eloheinu Melekh ha-olam borei atzei vesamim" ("Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates fragrant trees").

b) Over a fragrance emanating from herbs, one recites: "Barukh Ata Hashem Eloheinu Melekh ha-olam borei isvei vesamim" ("Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates fragrant herbs").

c) Over a pleasant fragrance emanating from a fruit, one recites: "Barukh Ata Hashem Eloheinu Melekh ha-olam ha-noten re'aḥ tov ba-peirot" ("Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who gives a pleasant fragrance to fruits").

d) Over a fragrance emanating from other things or from synthetic substances, one recites: "Barukh Ata Hashem Eloheinu Melekh ha-olam borei minei vesamim" ("Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates various kinds of spices").

e) Over a fragrance emanating from balsam oil, one recites: "Barukh Ata Hashem Eloheinu Melekh ha-olam borei shemen arev" ("Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates pleasant oil"). This oil is not available today.1

The blessing Minei Vesamim is unique in that, after the fact, it exempts all types of spices, for all of them are "kinds" of spices. Therefore, whenever there is a doubt regarding the type of fragrance, one recites Minei Vesamim (SA 216:2. See below in halakha 5 the definition of herbs and trees).

This is the reason that according to the Ashkenazic custom, at Havdala one recites Minei Vesamim over all types of spices: since many do not know what is a species of herb and what is a species of tree, there is a concern that they will err in their blessing, but if they always recite Minei Vesamim, they fulfill their obligation in any case. And according to the Sephardic custom, when the type of fragrance is known, one recites its own blessing over it (MB 297:1; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 31).

sections.title: The Blessing over Liquid and Synthetic Perfumes and over Tobacco
sections.html:
Over liquid perfumes that absorbed their fragrance from trees, one recites Atzei Vesamim. And if they absorbed their fragrance from herbs, Isvei Vesamim. And if they absorbed their fragrance from both, one recites Minei Vesamim (see SA 216:6; MB 19).

Over tobacco, many were accustomed not to recite a blessing, because it was intended to give a good feeling, whereas the fragrance with which it was infused was secondary to its main purpose. Also, its fragrance was generally weak, like the kinds of fragrance that have no source (as explained in the next halakha). But when a great deal of fragrance is put into tobacco, as is common today, the law depends on the aim of the one who takes it: if he took it for the sake of a good feeling and not for the sake of enjoying the fragrance, he should not recite a blessing. And if he took it for the sake of a good feeling and also for the sake of enjoying the fragrance, he is obligated to recite Minei Vesamim.2

Some say that one does not recite a blessing over a perfume made of synthetic substances, since by its nature it has no pleasant fragrance, and the fragrance was created in it only through an artificial process. However, in practice it seems that one must recite a blessing over it, for the chemical properties that made it possible to create the pleasant fragrance were created by God, and consequently one must recite Borei Minei Vesamim over its enjoyment.3

sections.title: Four Kinds of Pleasant Fragrance over Which One Does Not Recite a Blessing
sections.html:
Over four kinds of pleasant fragrance one does not recite a blessing: a) over a fragrance from which it is forbidden to derive benefit; b) over a fragrance intended to dispel bad odors; c) over a pleasant fragrance intended to scent other things; d) over a pleasant fragrance that has no source.

a) Over spices used for idolatry it is forbidden to recite a blessing. Since a person is forbidden to derive benefit from anything of idolatry, as it is stated (Devarim 13:18): "And nothing of the banned property shall cling to your hand," consequently even if he smelled it, it is forbidden to recite a blessing over it (SA 217:6). Likewise, one does not recite a blessing over the fragrance of a fruit that is orla, since it is forbidden to derive benefit from it (Radbaz; Knesset Ha-gedola).

Likewise, a man is forbidden to smell the perfume bottle of a woman whom he knows and who is not his wife, and if he smelled it, he should not recite a blessing. This is one of the safeguards that the Sages established in order to fortify the sanctity of marriage and to prevent a personal attachment between a man and a woman who is not his wife (SA 217:4; MB 16-17).

b) One recites a blessing over a pleasant fragrance intended for enjoyment, but if its purpose is to dispel bad odors, such as fragrances and sprays intended for bathrooms, even if they have a pleasant fragrance, one does not recite a blessing over them (Berakhot 53a; SA 217:2). And even one who smells them outside the bathroom and enjoys their pleasant fragrance should not recite a blessing, for since they were designated for removing bad odors and not for enjoyment, the Sages did not institute a blessing over them (Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 217:16, and Be'ur Halakha, s.v. "shel"). Likewise, one does not recite a blessing over deodorant intended to dispel the odor of sweat. Likewise, one does not recite a blessing over perfumed bath soaps, whose main purpose is the removal of dirt and bad odor from the body (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 217:5). However, if he decides to change the purpose of the fragrant substance, and to use it from then on for enjoyment and not for dispelling bad odors, he should recite a blessing over the enjoyment of its fragrance.

c) When the purpose of the pleasant fragrance is to scent other things, one does not recite a blessing over it, because it was not intended to be enjoyed in its own right. Therefore, one does not recite a blessing over laundry detergent containing a fragrant substance, or over kinds of fragrance placed in a clothes closet, because they are intended to impart a pleasant fragrance to the clothes, and not to be enjoyed separately for their own fragrance (SA 217:3). Likewise, one does not recite a blessing over a pleasant fragrance wafting from hand cream and aftershave, since they are intended to impart a pleasant fragrance to the body, and not to be enjoyed for their own fragrance. But over perfume one recites a blessing, since its fragrance is pleasant and strong, and it is intended for the enjoyment of its fragrance itself.

d) One does not recite a blessing over a fragrance that has no source, that is, when the source of the fragrant substance is not there, for since the fragrance we smell is about to dissipate in a short time, it does not have sufficient significance, and the Sages did not institute a blessing over it. Therefore, one does not recite a blessing over a pleasant fragrance wafting from clothes that absorbed their fragrance from fragrant laundry detergent or from fragrant substances placed in the closet. Likewise, one does not recite a blessing over the fragrance of perfume wafting from a person who perfumed himself (SA 217:3). Likewise, one who enters a cosmetics store and smells the fragrance still remaining in the air from bottles that were opened earlier in order to smell them does not recite a blessing, for since all the bottles are now closed, the fragrance has no source. Only one who opens a bottle in order to smell it should, when he enjoys the fragrance, recite a blessing over his enjoyment (Be'ur Halakha 217:3, s.v. "ela"). Likewise, a woman who perfumes herself should recite a blessing over the fragrance emanating from the perfume bottle.

sections.title: The Conditions Required for the Blessing over Fragrance
sections.html:
There are three types of fragrance: a) one intended for the enjoyment of a pleasant fragrance; b) one where the enjoyment of the fragrance accompanies its main purpose; c) one intended for the removal of bad odors.

a) One who passes by a garden in which plants that spread a pleasant fragrance were planted, since they are intended to give a pleasant fragrance to be enjoyed, if he wishes to enjoy their fragrance, he is obligated to recite a blessing. Likewise, one who passes by a shop or stall where kinds of fragrance intended to spread a pleasant fragrance are sold, such as soaps intended for this, if they are open and their pleasant fragrance wafts out and invites passersby to buy from them, they are intended for the enjoyment of fragrance, and anyone who passes by there, smells them and enjoys must recite a blessing, even if he does not buy from them (Berakhot 53a; SA 217:1). Likewise, one who enters a plant nursery that has fragrant seedlings should recite a blessing over them. For presumably the nursery owner wishes those who enter to enjoy their fragrance and buy the seedlings; it turns out that even now they are intended for the enjoyment of fragrance, and consequently anyone who enjoys them must recite a blessing. Likewise, one who enters a house and smells home incense or a perfume intended to spread a pleasant fragrance, since he enjoys it, must recite a blessing. Likewise, one who enters a car that has something that spreads a pleasant fragrance, since he enjoys it, must recite a blessing (SA 216:12; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 217:1).

b) There are things that have a pleasant fragrance, but this is not their purpose, and therefore even one who smells their pleasant fragrance, as long as he has not done an action in order to smell them, even though he enjoys their fragrance, is not permitted to recite a blessing. For example, one who passes by an orchard whose fragrance is pleasant, since the purpose of the orchard is to grow fruit, the pleasant fragrance wafting from it is secondary, and one does not recite a blessing over it. But if he approaches the flowers in order to smell them, since he did an action that gave the fragrance significance, it is no longer secondary and he is obligated to recite a blessing over his enjoyment. Likewise, one who passes by a field where fragrant trees and herbs are grown in order to market them, and likewise one who enters a factory that produces perfumes, since for the time being they are intended for a commercial purpose and not for the enjoyment of fragrance, even one who enjoys their fragrance should not recite a blessing. But if he approaches the fragrant branch or takes some of the perfumes in order to smell them, he is obligated to recite a blessing.

Likewise, there are fruits from which a pleasant fragrance sometimes wafts, such as an etrog and a lemon, and since their main purpose is for eating, one who enjoys their pleasant fragrance does not recite a blessing. But if he takes the fruit in order to smell it, its fragrance becomes significant for him, and he should recite over it Ha-noten Re'aḥ Tov Ba-peirot (SA 216:2).4

c) As we learned (in items b and c of the previous halakha), if the kind of fragrance is intended to dispel bad odors, or to give fragrance to something else, even if he takes it in order to enjoy its fragrance, he should not recite a blessing over it. Only if he changes its purpose, so that from then on it is intended for the enjoyment of fragrance, should he recite a blessing over it.

sections.title: The Various Blessings
sections.html:
One who errs and recites Isvei Vesamim over fragrant trees, or Atzei Vesamim over fragrant herbs, has not fulfilled his obligation, for trees are not herbs and herbs are not trees. Therefore, one must know well what is an herb and what is a tree. First, let us preface that in the language of the Sages a shrub is also called a tree, and therefore in practice most fragrant plants are trees. There are three conditions for a tree: a) it persists through its trunk from year to year; b) its branches or leaves grow out of the trunk or the stem and not from the roots; c) the trunk or stem is hard. When these three conditions are fulfilled, one recites Atzei Vesamim. In contrast, there are two conditions for a species of herb: a) its stem is soft; b) it must be sown anew each year, or its leaves grow out of its root. And in all intermediate situations, there is a doubt whether it is an herb or a tree, and one should recite Minei Vesamim.5

Let us mention several species whose blessing is Atzei Vesamim: myrtle, lemon cypress, jasmine, rosemary, clove, wormwood (shiba), honeysuckle, sage, flowers and leaves of trees, and lemon verbena (luiza) of the hard-stemmed variety.

Species whose blessing is Isvei Vesamim: rue (pigam), hyacinth, and narcissus, whose stem is soft.

Regarding mint and lemon verbena of the soft-stemmed variety, there is uncertainty, and therefore it is preferable to recite Minei Vesamim over them. Likewise, one who was brought a species of fragrant plant and has no easy way to clarify whether it is an herb or a tree should recite Minei Vesamim.

Spices are not considered fruits, since they are not eaten by themselves but only as an addition. Nor are they considered fragrant trees or fragrant herbs, since their main purpose is for taste and not for fragrance. Therefore, one who takes them in order to enjoy their fragrance recites Minei Vesamim (Rashbatz; see Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 216:12; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 34).

Many people enjoy the aroma of coffee, especially when it is being roasted and ground. One who passes by a shop where coffee is roasted or ground in order to sell it, since the shop owner wants people to smell its pleasant aroma and come to buy it, if he passes there and enjoys the aroma, he must recite Minei Vesamim. But one who passes by a coffee-processing factory, even if he enjoys the aroma, should not recite a blessing, since the purpose of the coffee there is commercial and not for the enjoyment of fragrance. Only if he takes some of the coffee in his hand or approaches it in order to smell it must he recite a blessing. And the same law applies to one who opens a new bag of coffee: if he took it in order to enjoy its aroma, he must recite a blessing. And even one who prepares a cup of coffee to drink, when the aroma of the coffee is weaker, if from the outset he intends also to enjoy the aroma of the coffee, he should recite Minei Vesamim. But if he did not think about this and began to drink, the aroma is secondary to the taste, and he should not recite a blessing over it.6
Over hot bread, even though its aroma is pleasant, one does not recite a blessing (Rema 216:14; MB 55), because its aroma is secondary to its importance. Furthermore, it is not an aroma that one enjoys for its own sake, but rather an aroma that arouses the appetite; it turns out that it is secondary to eating. Therefore one also does not recite a blessing over the aroma of roasted meat.

sections.title: Laws of the Blessing over Fragrance
sections.html:
One who suffers from a cold, or a person who has lost the sense of smell (anosmic), since he does not enjoy the pleasant fragrance, does not recite a blessing. One who is in doubt whether he senses the fragrance, or whether any fragrance remains in the perfume, should try to smell it, and if he senses a pleasant fragrance, he should intend to enjoy it and recite the blessing. One who is testing various perfumes in order to decide what to buy, as long as he is occupied with testing them, since his intention is not to enjoy, should not recite a blessing (Ben Ish Ḥai, Va-etḥanan 2; and see above 9:1, note 1).

If one took a kind of fragrance, recited a blessing over it and put it down, and afterwards wished to smell it again, since at the time of the first blessing he did not think that he would smell it again afterwards, he should recite the blessing again. And if, when he first recited the blessing, he intended to continue smelling it, as long as he is in his house, his first blessing is effective for him for the entire day. Likewise, if the fragrance was wafting in the house, even if he did not intend to continue smelling it, since in practice the fragrance continues to reach him, he need not recite the blessing again. And if he left his house for half an hour, this is an interruption, and when he returns and enjoys the fragrance, he should recite a blessing (SA 217:1; MA 3).

If one entered a place where there are several kinds of spices and he enjoys all of them together, he should recite Minei Vesamim. And if he wishes to smell each kind separately, he should intend not to enjoy all of them together, approach the different kinds of fragrance, and recite over each of them its own blessing.

If one interrupted by speaking about another matter between the blessing and the smelling, he has lost the blessing, and he must recite the blessing again before he enjoys the fragrance.

One who enjoys the smell of fuel or glue does not recite a blessing, for one recites a blessing only over something that most people consider a pleasant fragrance.

A person who does not enjoy a fragrance that most people consider pleasant does not recite a blessing, since he did not enjoy it.

One does not recite a blessing over the fragrance emanating from a pipe, for since it is forbidden to smoke because smoking is harmful to health, one should not recite a blessing over the enjoyment of smoking.

On Sukkot it is forbidden to smell the myrtles of the four species, for since their main purpose is the enjoyment of fragrance, when these myrtles were set aside for the mitzva of the four species, they became sanctified for their mitzva and it is forbidden to enjoy their fragrance (Sukka 37b). But over the etrog one should recite a blessing when one takes it specifically in order to smell it and not in order to fulfill the mitzva of taking the lulav.7
